1163.title: Yieldedness
1163.hook: Anabaptists speak of letting go of self-will
1163.howItsDone: Amish, Mennonite, Hutterite and other Anabaptist Christians speak of Gelassenheit, yielding self-will to God and to the community; it shapes their life together and their teaching of nonresistance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord's Day kept: Sunday set apart, whole. Your line was a day set apart.

A man is running across a frozen pond in the Netherlands, and behind him runs the man sent to catch him. He is an Anabaptist, and his faith is the charge. He makes it across. Behind him the ice cracks, and his pursuer goes through into the freezing water. The man stops, turns around, goes back out onto the ice, and pulls the officer out. Then he is taken. His name was Dirk Willems, and his story is told in the Martyrs Mirror, a book of Anabaptist martyr stories. A new week opens with the Anabaptists and the Quakers, and a German word: Gelassenheit.

Gelassenheit is hard to fit into one English word. Yieldedness comes close. Letting go. Letting be. Among the Amish, the Mennonites, the Hutterites and other Anabaptist churches, it names a whole way of standing in the world: giving up self-will, to God and to the community. Its pattern is Jesus in the garden the night before he died. He asks for the cup to pass from him, and then says, "nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Honest about what you want, and still letting go of it. It shows up in ordinary things: yielding to the church's shared way of life instead of standing out from it. In some communities plain clothes are part of that, not a costume but a quiet refusal to make the self the point. And it shows up in conflict. Anabaptist churches teach nonresistance, taking Jesus at his word in the Sermon on the Mount: "resist not evil." They hear a call to absorb harm instead of handing it back. Other churches read that verse differently, and teach that defending a neighbor can sometimes be right; Christians have held both views in good faith. Now go back to the pond. Self-will said keep running. Gelassenheit said turn around. It sounds like weakness, like giving up. On the ice it looked like the hardest kind of strength.

Bring to mind one disagreement you're in right now, the dishes, a plan, an old argument that keeps coming back, and notice where you want your way. Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and ask what it would cost to let just this one go. If you pray, you can say Jesus's words from the garden, not my will, but thine; if you don't, simply let your hands stay open.
Gelassenheit. The German word Anabaptists use for yieldedness: letting go of self-will, to God and to one another.
Your line: let go. Not losing every argument, just loosening your grip, so your hands are free. See you tomorrow.

1164.title: Nickel Mines (2006)
1164.hook: an Amish community forgave and embraced the family of the gunman who killed their children
1164.howItsDone: Amish Christians pray the Lord's Prayer in worship and at home and speak of forgiveness as a choice made ahead of time; after the Nickel Mines shooting, Amish neighbors visited and comforted the gunman's family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gelassenheit: yieldedness, letting go of self-will. Your line was let go.

Nickel Mines is a small village in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, in Amish farm country. One morning a man walked into its one-room Amish schoolhouse and shot the girls there. Some of them died, and so did he, by his own hand. There's no need to say more about that morning. What made people far away stop and look came after. Soon after, Amish neighbors went to the gunman's family, to say they forgave him, and to comfort his widow and children, who were grieving too. When he was buried, Amish mourners came and stood with that family.

Reporters asked how anyone could forgive so fast. The answer pointed back to something old. The Lord's Prayer runs through Amish worship and home life, and in the King James words it says, "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Right after the prayer, Jesus adds: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." Researchers who wrote a book about Nickel Mines, Amish Grace, heard Amish people describe forgiveness as decided long before the day it was needed, prayed into them over years of ordinary mornings. They didn't have to find it in the worst week of their lives. It had already been chosen, and when the day came, it chose them. It didn't mean the parents stopped grieving. Forgiving isn't forgetting, and it isn't saying the harm was small; the grief stayed, and had to be walked through. Nor was the matter simple for everyone else. Christians differ on how forgiveness works. Some point to Jesus in Luke's Gospel, "if he repent, forgive him," and hear forgiveness as waiting on repentance. Others point to Jesus on the cross: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." There, nobody had asked. Both readings are held in good faith. At Nickel Mines, the man could never ask. The forgiveness went to his family anyway: a visit, a hand, a presence at the grave.

Go gently with this one. Think of a family on the other side of some harm, the relatives of someone who hurt others, far away in the news or close to home: a mother, a brother, a child carrying a name they didn't choose. If you pray, hold them before God; if you don't, simply wish them peace, and if this touches a wound of your own, just rest and breathe. If it's too heavy, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Nickel Mines. A village in Amish country, and the name of a forgiveness that reached the family of the man who did the harm.
Your line: forgiveness chose them. It was prayed in long before it was needed. Rest well.

1165.title: Meeting for worship
1165.hook: Quakers sit in silence until someone is moved to speak
1165.howItsDone: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, Friends gather in silence and wait on God; anyone moved to speak stands and offers a few words, and the meeting closes with handshakes. Programmed Friends churches have a pastor, hymns and a sermon, often with a time of open silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nickel Mines: a forgiveness that went to the gunman's family. Your line was forgiveness chose them.

A plain room. Benches facing each other around the walls. No pulpit, no altar, nobody up front. People come in, sit down, and say nothing. Minutes pass. A cough. A bench creaks. A bird outside. Then a woman near the window stands, says a few sentences about something she's been carrying, and sits down again. Nobody answers her. The silence closes over her words like water. That's a Quaker meeting, of the kind Friends call unprogrammed. Quakers, the Religious Society of Friends, call that hour meeting for worship.

In an unprogrammed meeting there's no set order of service and no minister leading it. Friends gather in silence and wait on God together. That silence isn't a pause before the real thing starts. It is the real thing. Friends call it expectant waiting, the way you'd wait at a station for someone you know is coming. Behind it stands a promise of Jesus, "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them," and a line from the psalms: "Be still, and know that I am God." When someone feels moved by the Spirit to speak, they stand and give what Friends call ministry: a few words, a verse, a memory, sometimes a song. Then they sit, and the silence returns. Nobody replies or argues. Robert Barclay, an early Quaker writer, described coming into these silent meetings and feeling a hidden power among the people that touched his heart; as he gave way to it, the good in him was raised up. Friends still speak of a gathered meeting, when the whole room seems to go still together. When the hour is done, someone shakes a neighbor's hand, and the handshakes spread around the room. Not every Quaker meeting looks like this. Programmed Friends churches have a pastor, hymns and a sermon, often with a time of open silence inside the service. Both are Quaker, and both make room to wait on God.

Sit together if someone's nearby, or alone if not, and let the room go quiet. Don't fill the silence with a to-do list; wait, the way you'd wait for a friend at the station, and if a thought rises that seems worth keeping, hold it, then let it sink back into the quiet. If you pray, wait on God; if you don't, simply wait and listen.
Meeting for worship. The Quaker gathering in silence, waiting on God together, where anyone may be moved to speak.
Your line: expectant waiting. In that room, silence isn't empty. Same time tomorrow.

1166.title: Queries
1166.hook: Quakers ask themselves regular questions about truth, peace, simplicity, equality
1166.howItsDone: Quaker meetings keep written queries, questions about truth, peace, simplicity and equality, which are read aloud in meeting or pondered at home and answered inwardly, not out loud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting for worship: Friends waiting on God in silence. Your line was expectant waiting.

Do I keep my word? Read a question like that aloud to a room of Friends, and then leave it there. Not a question about doctrine. A question about the people in the room. The silence holds it. Nobody raises a hand. Nobody is graded. Each person carries it inward and answers it there, or doesn't yet. Friends call these questions queries. Quaker meetings keep written sets of them, about truth, peace, simplicity and equality, and come back to them again and again.

Why questions instead of rules? A rule tells you what to do and lets you stop thinking once you've done it. A question keeps working on you. Friends use queries to search their own lives, not to check off a list. It's an old instinct in the Bible. Paul writes to the Corinthians: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves." And Lamentations says: "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD." Queries gather around what Friends call testimonies, the shape their faith takes in daily life. Truth: Jesus said, "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay," and Friends have tried to let a plain word be enough, without oaths. Peace: how do you meet conflict? Simplicity: what are you carrying that you don't need? Equality: how do you treat people, all of them? That last one has a root. George Fox, an early Quaker preacher, urged Friends to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." Friends speak of that of God as a light in each person. To answer to it is to speak and act toward that light, even when the rest of the person is hard going. So a query on equality isn't really about manners. It's about whether you see that of God across the table. And a query isn't a test with a right answer. If you answer one quickly, it probably hasn't done its work yet.

Choose one of the four, truth, peace, simplicity or equality, and turn it into a plain question about your own week: where did I bend the truth, what am I holding that I don't need, whom did I treat as less? Don't rush to answer; let the question do the work. If you pray, hold it before God; if you don't, simply hold it honestly.
Queries. Questions Quakers ask themselves in meeting, about truth, peace, simplicity and equality, answered inwardly and never graded.
Your line: answer to that of God. There's a light in each person, even the hard ones. Until tomorrow.

1167.title: The class meeting
1167.hook: Methodists met weekly in small groups to watch over one another in love
1167.howItsDone: Early Methodists met weekly in small classes, where a leader asked each member how it was with their soul and they prayed for one another; some Methodist churches keep class meetings or similar small groups today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, queries: questions Friends carry into the silence. Your line was answer to that of God.

Once a week, a handful of people crowd into someone's front room. There's a leader, but no sermon. The leader turns to each person in turn and asks, in one form or another, the same question: how is it with your soul? And each one answers. A hard week at work. A temper that got away. A small joy. A prayer that won't come. Then they pray for one another, and go home. This was the Methodist class meeting, the small weekly gathering of John Wesley's early Methodists.

How are you is easy. Fine, thanks. How is it with your soul is harder, because it doesn't let you hide behind the weather. That question was the class meeting's whole job. Wesley's General Rules describe the people called Methodists as united to pray together, to hear encouragement, and "to watch over one another in love." Each society was split into small groups called classes, each with a leader. The Rules give the leader one task above the rest: to see each person once a week, "to inquire how their souls prosper," and then to advise, correct, comfort or encourage, as the person needed. Methodists tell a story about how it began. The classes started as a way to gather small weekly gifts for the society's needs. But a leader who knocks on doors each week starts hearing things: who's ill, who's drinking, who's quarreling at home. The collecting turned into caring. Watching over one another, in this sense, isn't spying. It's what Paul asks of the Galatians: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." And what Hebrews asks: "let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works." Ordinary people, not experts, holding each other to the life they'd chosen. Some Methodist churches have brought the class meeting back in new forms, and other Christians keep small groups of their own: Bible studies, cell groups, prayer partners. The old question still asks for an honest answer.

Ask yourself the class meeting's question: how is it with your soul? Not your inbox or your plans; let the answer be honest, even if it's tired, or I don't know. Then bring to mind one person you trust enough to ask the same thing, and if you pray, hold them before God, or simply hold them in mind with care.
The class meeting. The weekly Methodist small group, where a leader asked how each soul was doing, and the members watched over one another in love.
Your line: watch over one another. In love, never as spies. Rest well.

1168.title: The covenant prayer
1168.hook: Methodists renew their covenant each year: I am no longer my own, but yours
1168.howItsDone: Methodists hold a covenant service once a year, often around the new year, where the congregation renews its covenant with God and prays the covenant prayer together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the class meeting: how is it with your soul? Your line was watch over one another.

Joshua, old now, gathers the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He reminds them of everything God has done, and then he puts it to them plainly: choose whom you will serve. And he answers first, for himself: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." The people answer too, and that day, the book says, Joshua made a covenant with them. A promise already made, made again. Methodists do something like that once a year, at a covenant service, renewing their promise to God in words that aren't easy to say.

Covenant is a word the Bible keeps coming back to. In Hebrew it's berit, and it runs from Noah to Abraham to Sinai. Jeremiah looks ahead to a new one, where God says, "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." Not carved on stone this time. Written inside. John Wesley took up a yearly renewal of that covenant from Puritan writers before him, and gave it to the Methodists. The prayer Methodists say today is short, and it's hard. It begins with today's line: I am no longer my own, but yours. Then it hands everything over, the pleasant and the painful together. Put me to doing, or to suffering. Use me, or set me aside. Let me be full, or empty. Let me have all things, or nothing. It isn't asking for suffering. It's refusing to make faithfulness depend on comfort. Plenty of promises come with conditions; this one tries to have none. Paul gives the ground for it: "ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price." Christian teaching reads that price as Christ's own life. And the prayer doesn't end in loss. At the close, the one who gave everything away hears that God is theirs too, like the Song of Songs: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." Why say it every year? Because people drift. A covenant, like a marriage, gets spoken again so it isn't forgotten.

Notice what you'd find hardest to hand over: a plan, a comfort, a person, being needed. Don't argue with it; just see it. If you pray, say the prayer's first line slowly, I am no longer my own, but yours, and stop there; if you don't, name the thing once, quietly, and let it sit there without grabbing it back.
The covenant prayer. The Methodist prayer of yielding everything to God, said each year when the covenant is renewed.
Your line: no longer my own. Full or empty, the promise holds. See you at the table tomorrow.

1169.title: The love feast
1169.hook: a simple shared meal of bread and water with testimonies
1169.howItsDone: At a Methodist love feast, plain bread and water are shared and people tell what God has done in their lives; Moravians hold a lovefeast with buns and coffee during singing, and the Church of the Brethren keeps a love feast with footwashing, a meal and communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the covenant prayer: a promise made again, with nothing held back. Your line was no longer my own.

In Corinth, the church's shared meal has gone wrong. Some arrive early and eat their own suppers before the others get there. Paul doesn't soften it: "one is hungry, and another is drunken." A meal meant to make them one family was splitting them into rich and poor. And still the early church kept eating together. Jude's short letter mentions their "feasts of charity," in the King James words. Charity there is love. Love feasts. Methodists, Moravians, Brethren and others still keep a meal by that name.

Acts describes the first believers "breaking bread from house to house," and says they "did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." Meat there just means food. A table where everybody eats. John Wesley learned the love feast from the Moravians, brought it into Methodism, and kept it plain on purpose: simple bread or cake, and water, passed from hand to hand, with a shared cup. Nothing to show off. Corinth's problem would be hard to repeat at a table like that. Then came the real meal: testimony. People stood and told what God had done in their lives that year, that week. A healing, a rescue, a long night, a turning point. Bread for the body, and a story for everyone else to chew on. Methodists keep it distinct from the Lord's Supper: it isn't communion; it's fellowship. Other churches keep their own forms. Moravians hold a lovefeast with sweet buns and coffee, served while the congregation sings. The Church of the Brethren keeps a love feast with footwashing, a full meal and then communion, following Jesus at the Last Supper. Different tables, the same old word. This whole week has been rooms like this: Gelassenheit, a village that forgave, Quaker silence and the queries carried into it, how is it with your soul, a covenant renewed, and now bread and a story. Anabaptists, Quakers, Methodists: ordinary people carrying the faith together, around a plain table.

Remember one table that fed you more than food: a kitchen, a hospital tray, a picnic, a stranger's dinner. Who was there, and what story got told? If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, simply thank the people who were there, wherever they are now.
The love feast. A plain shared meal, bread and water, with stories of what God has done, kept by Methodists, Moravians, Brethren and others.
Your line: bread and a story. Plain food, true words, everyone fed. That's the week.
